armF.summary: Some calls through Meta’s Muse were handled by human contractors without users being properly informed.
armF.prompt:
Below is a finished English news feature article (already translated from Japanese, no section headings). Write ONE short, natural sentence that captures the core of the story, in a way a listener can understand by hearing it just once.

Requirements:
- Exactly one sentence.
- Understandable on a single listen.
- Do not pack in multiple separate points; focus on the single most important point or twist of the story.
- Do not add any new fact, conclusion, or lesson that is not already stated in the article below.
- Keep who did what to whom, and what exactly it applied to, the same as in the Japanese source article and the Ledger below.

As a rough guide only (Trial-only guidance, not a strict rule): aim for one main clause with at most one subordinate clause, roughly 12-18 words.

Output only the sentence itself, nothing else (no quotation marks, no label like "In one line:", no Markdown heading markup).

[Article]
# Muse’s Phone Calls: Humans Step Out from the Wings

Haircut appointments, checking a store’s stock, getting price estimates from service providers. It was reported that Muse has a feature that can call businesses and stores in the United States and take care of these tasks. But on some calls, trained contract workers—not AI—made the calls and completed the conversations. This was a test of “human concierges.”

To use a stage comparison, the setup was that human stand-ins could also appear in scenes where AI was supposed to show up. But the main point this time was not how well the stand-ins did their jobs. It was whether people were properly told who was handling the calls.

Meta employees were concerned that, during calls, users’ sensitive information could be shared unintentionally with contract workers at call centers. This does not mean that an actual information leak was confirmed. The problem was that the test, in which contract workers made calls, began without proper disclosure, even though information could be shared with people.

When people ask AI to take care of a task, they may want to know more than whether the task gets done. Who is speaking on the other end of the phone, and who can hear their information? Even if Muse is onstage, if there is a human on the phone, people should be able to use the service knowing that.

A vice president in the relevant Meta division admitted that it was a mistake to start the test with contract workers making calls without proper disclosure. Meta then rolled back the human concierge feature for the time being. If humans are going to appear behind the scenes of AI, the audience should be told who is in the cast before the curtain rises. This whole affair was also a case of one obvious thing being left unsaid.

[Japanese source article]
Museの電話、舞台袖から人間が登場

散髪の予約、店の在庫確認、業者からの見積もり。Museには、米国内の企業や店に電話して、こうした用事を頼める機能があると報じられました。ところが電話の一部では、AIではなく、訓練を受けた人間の契約スタッフが電話をかけ、相手とのやり取りを完了させていました。これが「人間コンシェルジュ」のテストです。

舞台にたとえるなら、AIが出るはずの場面に、人間の代役も登場する仕掛け。今回の見どころは、代役の仕事ぶりではありません。誰が電話を担当するのか、適切に伝えられていたかです。

Metaの従業員は、電話中に利用者の機微な情報が、コールセンターの契約スタッフへ意図せず共有される可能性を懸念しました。ここで、実際に情報漏えいが確認されたという話ではありません。問題になったのは、情報が人に伝わる可能性があるのに、契約スタッフが電話するテストを適切な開示なしに始めたことです。

AIに用事を頼むとき、利用者が知りたいのは、用事が済むかどうかだけではないかもしれません。電話の向こうで誰が話し、誰が情報を聞くのか。舞台の表側がMuseでも、電話口に人間がいるなら、そのことを知ったうえで利用できるようにしてほしいところです。

Metaの担当部門の副社長は、適切な開示なしに契約スタッフが電話するテストを始めたのはミスだったと認めました。そして、人間コンシェルジュ機能を当面ロールバックしました。AIの舞台裏から人間が登場するなら、幕が上がる前に、その配役を観客にも知らせる。今回の騒動は、そんな当たり前の一言が欠けていた話でもあります。

armR.final_summary: Meta rolled back Muse’s human-concierge test after admitting it began without properly disclosing that contractors handled some calls.
armR.final_text:
# Muse’s Phone Calls: Humans Step Out from the Wings

Haircut appointments, checking a store’s stock, getting price estimates from service providers. It was reported that Muse has a feature that can call businesses and stores in the United States and take care of these tasks. But on some calls, trained contract workers—not AI—made the calls and completed the conversations. This was a test of “human concierges.”

To use a stage comparison, the setup was that human stand-ins could also appear in scenes where AI was supposed to show up. But the main point this time was not how well the stand-ins did their jobs. It was whether people were properly told who was handling the calls.

Meta employees were concerned that, during calls, users’ sensitive information could be shared unintentionally with contract workers at call centers. This does not mean that an actual information leak was confirmed. The problem was that the test, in which contract workers made calls, began without proper disclosure, even though information could be shared with people.

When people ask AI to take care of a task, they may want to know more than whether the task gets done. Who is speaking on the other end of the phone, and who can hear their information? Even if Muse is onstage, if there is a human on the phone, people should be able to use the service knowing that.

A vice president in the relevant Meta division admitted that it was a mistake to start the test with contract workers making calls without proper disclosure. Meta then rolled back the human concierge feature for the time being. If humans are going to appear behind the scenes of AI, the audience should be told who is in the cast before the curtain rises. This whole affair was also a case of one obvious thing being left unsaid.

## In one line
Meta rolled back Muse’s human-concierge test after admitting it began without properly disclosing that contractors handled some calls.
